title: As US measles cases rise, biotech firms start developing new treatments
gist: With US measles cases at a 35-year high and already past last year's 2,289 by July versus 285 in all of 2024, Invivyd, the La Jolla Institute, and Vanderbilt with Saravir Biopharma are developing monoclonal antibodies for treatment and short-term protection. None have entered human trials, funding is hard because infectious-disease drugs are poor commercial products, and the open question is whether vaccine-refusing families would accept an antibody at all.

insights.claim: US measles cases have hit a 35-year high, already surpassing last year's 2,289 cases by July, against just 285 cases in all of 2024.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An eightfold-plus escalation in two years establishes the demand case for measles therapeutics that did not exist before.
insights.quote: the US had already surpassed last year’s 2,289 measles cases, and it’s only July. For comparison, there were just 285 cases in all of 2024.
insights.locator: Fueled by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah

insights.claim: Large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah are driving the 2026 case surge.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration means state-level vaccination policy is the actionable variable, not national averages.
insights.locator: Fueled by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah

insights.claim: Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 percent of a community must receive both vaccine doses to protect immunocompromised people and infants under 12 months, and rates have dipped well below that in many US locations.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The 95 percent threshold is the hard trigger for outbreak risk; local coverage data is the leading indicator.
insights.locator: Because measles is so contagious

insights.claim: Some disease models predict measles could become endemic in the US within 25 years even at current state-level vaccination rates, implying a persistent rather than episodic market.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Endemicity would convert measles therapeutics from outbreak-response products into a recurring revenue category.
insights.quote: Some disease models predict that measles could become endemic in the US in the next 25 years, even at current state-level vaccination rates.
insights.locator: I think this is a real opportunity to solve a public health problem

insights.claim: There is currently no measles-specific treatment, only supportive care, and vitamin A is given because the virus depletes it but has no effect on the virus itself.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A genuine therapeutic void means first movers face no incumbent standard of care to displace.
insights.locator: Without a measles-specific treatment, doctors rely on supportive care

insights.claim: Invivyd, whose chief medical officer is epidemiologist Michael Mina, is developing a measles monoclonal antibody that has not yet been tested in humans, with the company compiling data for Food and Drug Administration sign-off on clinical trials.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Invivyd is the closest named public-market proxy for measles therapeutics, still at pre-IND stage.
insights.locator: Invivyd is developing a type of therapy for measles

insights.claim: Monoclonal antibodies given by IV or injection could provide short-term protection lasting up to a few months to high-risk individuals during a local measles outbreak, mirroring their COVID-era use in immunocompromised patients.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The product is outbreak-triggered prophylaxis, so revenue is lumpy and tied to local case surges rather than annual demand.
insights.locator: Given via IV or injection, monoclonal antibodies were widely used

insights.claim: La Jolla Institute for Immunology president Erica Ollmann Saphire published a May study describing human antibodies that block measles infection, with an infusion producing a 500-fold lower viral load in rodents.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A 500-fold viral load reduction in animals is the efficacy signal that would justify moving to human trials.
insights.quote: An infusion of these antibodies resulted in a 500-fold lower viral load in rodents.
insights.locator: At the La Jolla Institute for Immunology

insights.claim: Vanderbilt University has partnered with small biotech Saravir Biopharma, with James Crowe pursuing a two-antibody combination to drastically reduce the chance the measles virus mutates to evade treatment.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Combination design is the standard escape-mutation hedge and raises cost of goods, a key margin consideration.
insights.locator: The university has partnered with small biotech firm Saravir Biopharma

insights.claim: James Crowe says the isolated antibodies are so potent they strongly inhibit the virus and could be formulated as a single long-acting shot rather than an infusion.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Single-shot formulation would collapse administration costs and make community-level deployment feasible.
insights.quote: The antibodies that we have isolated are so potent, they strongly inhibit the virus.
insights.locator: James Crowe, an immunologist and director

insights.claim: Crowe's group has been systematically making human antibodies against viruses most likely to cause future pandemics and happened to be mid-way through the measles work when US cases intensified last year.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Pre-positioned pandemic antibody libraries shorten response time and are a strategic asset worth valuing separately.
insights.locator: His group has been systematically making human antibodies

insights.claim: Drugs for infectious diseases are not usually big money-makers because outbreaks are sporadic and treatment courses are short, making measles therapeutics a hard sell to the pharma partners needed to fund multimillion-dollar trials.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The funding gap, not the science, is the binding constraint; public or philanthropic capital is the likely swing factor.
insights.quote: Drugs for infectious diseases aren’t usually big money-makers because of the sporadic nature of outbreaks and short treatment courses.
insights.locator: A key step toward getting these treatments into human trials

insights.claim: Manufacturing monoclonal antibodies at scale is a costly and complex process and is identified as a key gating step before human trials.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: CDMO capacity and cost of goods determine whether any of these programs can reach outbreak-scale supply.
insights.locator: A key step toward getting these treatments into human trials will be manufacturing

insights.claim: In early 2022 the US government spent $855 million for 1.7 million doses of the COVID monoclonal antibody Evusheld, and patients still faced hundreds of dollars in out-of-pocket administration costs despite the drug being free.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: That roughly $500-per-dose government procurement price is the best available benchmark for pricing a measles antibody.
insights.quote: the US government spent $855 million for 1.7 million doses of Evusheld
insights.locator: Monoclonal antibodies could also be costly

insights.claim: The Evusheld antibody combination was created in just 25 days by Vanderbilt scientists, showing discovery speed is not the bottleneck in antibody development.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: If discovery takes weeks, timelines are set entirely by funding, manufacturing and regulatory steps.
insights.quote: The monoclonal antibody combination that became Evusheld was created in just 25 days by scientists at Vanderbilt University
insights.locator: Monoclonal antibodies could also be costly for patients

insights.claim: Erica Ollmann Saphire argues a tool to prevent or treat measles is still cheaper than managing an outbreak or a case of fatal encephalitis in a child, framing the investment case in avoided public health cost.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Cost-offset framing is how these programs get public funding when private pharma economics fail.
insights.quote: A tool by which you could prevent or treat disease is still cheaper than managing an outbreak or managing a case of fatal encephalitis in a child.
insights.locator: I think this is a real opportunity

insights.claim: Regulators will have to resolve how to evaluate measles antibodies in trials because new drugs are normally tested in adults first, yet measles complications disproportionately hospitalize unvaccinated children.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Pediatric-first trial design is a regulatory novelty that could add years to the timeline for these programs.
insights.locator: Once these monoclonal antibodies are ready for human testing

insights.claim: Georgia State University researchers identified an oral antiviral that lowered viral load and kept all treated animals alive in rats, ferrets and dogs infected with related orthoparamyxoviruses, but it has not been tested in people.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An oral antiviral would be far cheaper to distribute than antibodies but is at an earlier and less proven stage.
insights.locator: Researchers at Georgia State University identified an oral antiviral drug

insights.claim: Antivirals are structurally disadvantaged for measles because their effect is short-lived and they must be given very soon after infection or symptom onset, and drugs toxic enough to kill viruses often have unpleasant side effects.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Narrow treatment windows favor the antibody approach for prophylaxis even at higher cost.
insights.locator: Antivirals could also be used as a strategy to treat measles

insights.claim: Michael Mina hopes vaccine-refusing families will accept a monoclonal antibody because it is a molecule the body creates naturally, an explicit marketing framing to bypass anti-vaccine sentiment.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Whether that framing works determines the real addressable population, since the vaccinated do not need the product.
insights.quote: this is a molecule that our bodies create naturally
insights.locator: While anti-vaccine sentiment is driving the current outbreaks

insights.claim: During the Utah measles outbreak some parents refused to let doctors give their children immune globulin, a directly analogous antibody product, which is evidence against the acceptance thesis.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Real-world refusal of an existing antibody product is the strongest available datapoint on adoption risk for these programs.
insights.locator: But during the Utah measles outbreak, some parents have refused

insights.claim: Anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. leading the Department of Health and Human Services, where he has cast doubt on vaccines and other established treatments.
insights.speaker: WIRED
entities: Department of Health and Human Services
insights.so_what: Federal health leadership is a headwind to both vaccination rates and uptake of any new countermeasure.
insights.locator: And anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream

insights.claim: James Crowe predicts hundreds of thousands of measles cases and deaths, arguing there is urgency to finishing the treatment work as vaccination rates continue to decline.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A researcher forecasting six-figure case counts is the tail scenario that would force emergency federal procurement.
insights.quote: I think there’s going to be hundreds of thousands of cases
insights.locator: Crowe says it’s important that work on measles treatments
